A 65-year-old man presents with four months of low-grade fever and malaise. He also says he has lost 9 kg (20 lb) during this period and suffers from extreme fatigue. Past medical history is significant for a mitral valve replacement five years ago. His temperature is 38.1°C (100.6°F), respirations are 22/min, pulse is 102/min, and blood pressure is 138/78 mm Hg. On physical examination, there is a new onset 2/6 holosystolic murmur, loudest in the apical area of the precordium. Which of the following organisms is the most likely cause of this patient’s condition?

Options:
A. *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*
B. *Bartonella henselae*
C. HACEK group organisms
D. *Candida albicans*
E. Beta-hemolytic streptococci
F. *Staphylococcus aureus*
G. Coagulase-negative *Staphylococcus spp.*
H. *Pseudomonas* aeruginosa
I. *Streptococcus bovis*
J. *Enterococcus*

Presentation: A 43-year-old woman with a history of aortic valve replacement three years ago presented with a 20-day history of fever and night sweats. Physical examination revealed an axillary temperature of 38.5°C, heart rate of 90/min, blood pressure of 90/70 mmHg, and a diastolic murmur (2/4) at the aortic area. Routine chemistry panel and haemogram were within normal limits. C-reactive protein (CRP) level was 28 g/dl (normal <5) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was 30 mm/hour. She had undergone silicon mammoplasty nine months ago and dental extraction four months ago. Three months ago, she was treated with ceftriaxone and gentamicin for four weeks. After one month of discharge, she experienced fever and night sweats again. On the second day of the current hospitalization, painful nodules were observed on the pad of the right index finger. Empirical treatment with ampicillin-sulbactam and gentamicin was initiated.. Confirmed diagnosis: Staphylococcus warnerii prosthetic valve endocarditis. Differential diagnosis includes: Staphylococcus warnerii prosthetic valve endocarditis.

Presentation: A 64-year-old woman presented with right back pain localized around the right costovertebral angle, which began 6 days prior to admission. She visited the emergency outpatient unit 5 days prior to admission. The pain did not migrate, and she had no fever or other symptoms. She had undergone an aortic valve replacement 7 months earlier without postsurgical complications, and cefazolin was administered for 3 days during the perioperative period. Her body temperature was 36.9°C, with blood pressure readings of 114/74 mm Hg on the right arm and 114/81 mm Hg on the left arm. Physical examination showed no conjunctival hemorrhage or cardiac murmur. Laboratory tests indicated an elevated white blood cell count of 8,830/µL and a C-reactive protein level of 10.12 mg/dL. Enhanced CT of the chest and abdomen revealed no abnormalities. Blood cultures were performed due to her medical history and physical examination findings. Four days prior to admission, methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus epidermidis (MRSE) was detected in two sets of blood cultures. Despite recommendations for hospitalization, she chose to go home. Repeated blood cultures again showed MRSE in two sets, leading to her admis. Confirmed diagnosis: Prosthetic Valve Endocarditis. Differential diagnosis includes: Prosthetic Valve Endocarditis.

Presentation: A 53-year-old male patient had a mitral valve replacement using a Starr Edwards metal valve. Post-surgery, he experienced acute renal failure and required temporary hemodialysis via a vascular catheter for 36 days. The longest duration a single catheter was used was 13 days. Cultures from four removed vascular catheter tips showed the presence of diphtheroids and coagulase-negative staphylococci, typically considered normal skin flora. During this period, the patient developed a low-grade fever, which subsided after changing the catheters. Blood cultures did not show any growth.. Confirmed diagnosis: Prosthetic Valve Endocarditis caused by Corynebacterium jeikeium. Differential diagnosis includes: Prosthetic Valve Endocarditis caused by Corynebacterium jeikeium.

Presentation: An 80-year-old female was admitted in March 2012 presenting with fever, low blood pressure, and confusion. Her medical history includes aortic valve replacement with a biological prosthesis and double coronary artery bypass performed in April 2011. Upon admission, blood cultures identified the presence of Staphylococcus lugdunensis. The patient was treated with oxacillin, which led to the resolution of her fever. CT/FDG-PET revealed a diffuse uptake on prosthetic valve (SUVmax 4.2). Two weeks after hospital admission a new TEE showed a peri-valve tissue abscess with aortic vegetation.. Confirmed diagnosis: Prosthetic Valve Endocarditis. Differential diagnosis includes: Prosthetic Valve Endocarditis.

The most common indication for TKR is osteoarthritis (OA). In 2018, 96.2% of primary knee replacements were conducted solely due to osteoarthritis. TKR helps to improve quality of life and function in end-stage, symptomatic osteoarthritis patients. However, 10–34% of TKR patients receive adverse pain outcomes between three months and five years following surgery and around 20% of TKR patients experience more knee pain and swelling than before surgery. Despite advancements in surgical techniques, prostheses, pain control, and medical care, there is evidence to suggest worsening pain and functional scores of some patients over time following TKR surgery.

 Hot, swollen, single joint = septic until proven otherwise → arthrocentesis
 Fever with joint complaints (septic arthritis, endocarditis)
 Prosthetic joint with new pain/swelling (prosthetic joint infection)
 IV drug use + joint pain (hematogenous seeding)
 Polyarthritis + new murmur (endocarditis)
 Pediatric arthritis + fever + rash (consider Kawasaki disease , rheumatic fever , JIA)

The most common indication for TKR is osteoarthritis (OA). In 2018, 96.2% of primary knee replacements were conducted solely due to osteoarthritis. TKR helps to improve quality of life and function in end-stage, symptomatic osteoarthritis patients. However, 10–34% of TKR patients receive adverse pain outcomes between three months and five years following surgery and around 20% of TKR patients experience more knee pain and swelling than before surgery. Despite advancements in surgical techniques, prostheses, pain control, and medical care, there is evidence to suggest worsening pain and functional scores of some patients over time following TKR surgery.
